experience: Personal finance
takeaway: Used an Excel spreadsheet to manually track expenses but lost motivation after a while.
quotes: So back in around February I got motivated to create a spreadsheet by using those templates they provide for you, as a way to keep track of my personal finances. First week or two I was actually tracking everything, however by the third week I ended up getting lazy and just stopped.
Mostly updating the spreadsheet every day and having to record my expenses became a hassle.

experience: Personal finance and work finance
takeaway: A finance professional did not stick with manual categorization since it required daily manual updating.
quotes: Last year I tried switching from a budgeting app I normally use to a spreadsheet to have more control over what categories I could track. I ended up creating a spreadsheet with like 15 categories, but after a month I got busier like usual and I didn’t have the time to categorize every transaction I did.
I went back to using the budgeting app that is auto synced with my accounts. It automatically gives me metrics and categorizes things for me.

role: Owner of a stair construction contracting company
experience: Personal finance and business finance
takeaway: Tracks business and personal expenses consistently in a spreadsheet and did not find budgeting apps useful.
quotes: I don’t really have one, I’ve always been consistent with tracking all the business and personal expenses I have.
I’ve tried to look into apps that can handle this for me, but they seem too complicated for me to learn and I’d rather just stick to a simple Excel sheet I created and understand.
I was stuck with just using my own spreadsheet since the apps I looked into felt built for people with salary.

experience: Personal finance
takeaway: Relies on built-in credit card categorization and simple bank metrics; no felt problem.
quotes: It was pretty convenient, but I didn’t really want to pay the monthly subscription. Either way I have a Discover credit card and it already categorizes my purchases for free.
It wasn’t difficult, it was more paying for something that I knew I could just do by myself and eyeball it.

experience: Personal finance
takeaway: Replaced expense logging with a physical cash envelope system paired with a simple spreadsheet.
quotes: I once tried using a personal budgeting template from Excel but I got tired of having to manually write down every purchase I did or money I saved.
Having to write down every expense was the difficult part, however for saving money it was easier and more fun to visually see my money being placed in a booklet.

role: College student who regularly goes to the gym
experience: Has attempted to lose weight while tracking calories and protein
takeaway: Frequently discovers too late in the day that they are below their protein target, and finds consistent tracking difficult without meal preparation.
quotes: I mostly decide when I’m already hungry.
I would check the app at night and realize I was still like 40 grams short.
The best week I had was when I meal prepped everything on Sunday.

experience: Has attempted to gain weight and muscle while working a physically demanding job
takeaway: Struggles to eat enough while bulking because an unpredictable work schedule makes meal planning difficult, and calorie shortages are often discovered late.
quotes: I don’t really know before I eat everything whether it’s going to be enough for the day.
If I knew after lunch that I was way behind, I could add a shake or bigger dinner.
There have been days where I check at night and I’m still 700 or 800 calories under.

experience: Has tracked macros while trying to maintain weight and improve body composition
takeaway: Stopped detailed macro tracking because it became tedious; would prefer planning meals and projected macros before eating.
quotes: It started making eating feel like homework.
Probably being able to plan the meals first instead of entering everything after I already ate it.

experience: Has attempted weight loss while working long and irregular shifts
takeaway: An irregular work schedule makes daily food tracking difficult and can lead to unintentionally eating too little earlier and overeating later.
quotes: My weight goal affected what I chose, but convenience affected it more.
If I barely eat all day, I get really hungry later.
Trying to log everything during a 12-hour shift wasn’t realistic for me.

experience: Recently began trying to gain muscle and increase protein intake
takeaway: Understands their general nutrition goal but has difficulty translating macro targets into actual meals, and often realizes deficiencies only after eating.
quotes: I understand what my goal is, but I don’t always know what meals I should eat to actually reach it.
I had enough calories, but a lot of them came from snacks.

role: Participant, role not recorded on the grid sheet

I usually don’t look for events, they just come to me on my feed, I don’t actively look for events.
Not as often, because I don’t actively look for things to do, so I often just don’t find out at all.

role: Participant, role not recorded on the grid sheet

role: Participant, role not recorded on the grid sheet

It happens to me often.

role: Participant, role not recorded on the grid sheet

role: Participant, role not recorded on the grid sheet
quotes: It’s mostly by chance if I ever come across something, I don’t even know what to look for most of the times.

Not too often, because I end up not hearing about the events at all, so I don’t even notice I miss them.

role: Participant, role not recorded on the grid sheet

Losing a bunch of money because I don’t know what I’m doing.

role: Participant, role not recorded on the grid sheet

Market crashes. I work hard for my paycheck, so the idea of watching my account drop like 20% in a week gives me anxiety.
I think if it can clearly explain things to beginners I would try it out.

role: Participant, role not recorded on the grid sheet

I downloaded an app once that was kind of like flash cards, but that’s about it.

role: Participant, role not recorded on the grid sheet

If it clearly proves to me step by step that I won’t lose all my money.

role: Participant, role not recorded on the grid sheet

The time spent having to research and learn everything while having to work. It’s like a second full-time job.
I downloaded one once, but there was too much finance jargon, I didn’t know what I was reading.

role: Participant, role not recorded on the grid sheet

role: Participant, role not recorded on the grid sheet

role: Participant, role not recorded on the grid sheet

experience: No prior experience with the problem area

I think it would probably be discouraging for me. I’d feel pressured to keep up with it, and I already struggle with getting motivated.
Honestly, I just eat whatever’s at home. It depends on what my mom cooks.

experience: No prior experience with the problem area
takeaway: Finds it boring to track meals or macros, but would try eating less junk and more protein.
quotes: I’ve wanted to track my food before, but I never really committed to it. I just try not to eat too much junk food.
I think tracking could be encouraging at first, but I’d probably get bored of it after a while.
Day to day, it’s mostly what’s easy to make or what’s available.

experience: Eats healthy meals a few times a week
takeaway: Tracks meals a few times a week and does not track macros; an app could push her a little further toward tracking macros.
quotes: I started tracking my food because I wanted to make sure I wasn’t overeating.
No, I don’t track my macros, just my meals.
It’s encouraging for me. It allows me to track my calories without getting too strict.

experience: Somewhat tracks daily protein intake, but no diet in place
takeaway: Works out regularly and does not track food, but eats a relatively balanced diet; could benefit from an app that suggests other healthy foods.
quotes: I’ve tracked my protein a few times just to make sure I’m getting enough. It’s more casual for me.
It’s encouraging. It makes it easier to stay on top of my diet, but it does get annoying having to track.

experience: Meal preps regularly, but does not track macros
takeaway: Enjoys meal prepping but does not like to track macros.
quotes: I started meal prepping because it saves time and keeps me from eating out too much. So yeah, I like to meal prep, but I don’t really track my macros.
All my meals are the same. When I prep them, I don’t make different ones, it’s the same thing every day for the week.

experience: Has used a fitness and food tracking app before
takeaway: Found it simple to start using a food tracking app toward a fitness goal, but only found it encouraging while keeping up with it; wants to track protein, calories and food quality.
quotes: Since I was 17 I have been wanting to track my food intake. The process was fairly simple at first since my parents helped me and it was simple to track the food and calories I was eating with apps like MyFitnessPal and Apple Health.
I think it is encouraging when you actually stick with it on a day-to-day basis but it is discouraging when you do not keep up with it.

experience: Has used food tracking apps to meet fitness and health goals
takeaway: Has found a food tracking app a helpful tool for fitness goals; it has encouraged them to feel better about their eating habits while allowing flexibility.
quotes: I used an app called MyFitnessPal and it made it fairly easy since a lot of the items I was eating were in the system already with all their nutrition information.
I see it more as encouraging because it makes it a lot easier to know what I have to eat more of to meet my goals.

A lot of times I also choose things that I’m craving, even if it doesn’t meet my goals, since I think having meals and snacks that make me happy is also important to maintain a balanced and sustainable diet.

experience: Has used a food tracking app to meet their recommended caloric intake
takeaway: Used a food tracking app to make sure she was eating enough; finds the app mostly discouraging, and encouraging on the days she hits her calorie and protein targets.
quotes: I had to consult an app because as a person who doesn’t know much about conversions of body weight to height to calories and stuff, I just found it easier to consult an app.

There is never a day for me where I do exactly a hundred percent what I should be doing without going over or under the recommended calories I need to eat. So I think it can be mostly discouraging, but sometimes when I do get it right, it’s encouraging.

experience: Used MyFitnessPal to track food last semester
takeaway: Tracked calories in MyFitnessPal to lose weight and found seeing the numbers encouraging, but stopped logging consistently once classes got busy; picks food mainly on price.
quotes: It was easy at first, but after a while I would forget to enter some meals, especially when I was busy with classes.
I think it was encouraging because I could actually see when I was eating too much. Sometimes it was annoying having to enter everything though.
Price is probably the biggest thing for me.

role: UTEP college student who goes to the gym regularly
experience: Tracked protein and calories for a few weeks after starting to go to the gym more
takeaway: Tracked protein and calories to gain muscle and found it encouraging because it replaced guessing, but consistency dropped during exams; daily choices come down to protein, price, and how filling the food is.
quotes: I did pretty well for a few weeks, but I stopped being as consistent during exams.
It was encouraging for me because it gave me something to follow. I knew if I was getting enough protein instead of just guessing.

experience: Tracked meals for about a month, mostly written down in a notes app
takeaway: Tracked meals loosely in a notes app to cut back on fast food and found it both helpful and discouraging, since a bad day felt like failure; eats around whatever the schedule allows.
quotes: I didn’t use an app every day. Sometimes I just wrote down my meals in my notes app. It helped, but I wasn’t very strict about it.
It helped me notice my eating habits, but sometimes seeing everything I ate made me feel like I had messed up if I had a bad day.

experience: Used a tracking app for two to three weeks over the summer
takeaway: Tracked for a few weeks to maintain weight and found it encouraging for awareness, but dropped the measuring part because homemade food was hard to estimate; now decides based on what is already at home.
quotes: The hardest part was figuring out the calories when I ate homemade food.
I didn’t like having to measure everything, so I eventually stopped doing that part.
I think about what I have at home first because I don’t want to spend money eating out.

experience: Used a tracking app for about a week after friends started tracking calories
takeaway: Tried tracking for about a week because friends were doing it and quit because logging snacks and drinks felt like extra work; chooses food based on cost and how much break time is left between classes.
quotes: I stopped because I kept forgetting to log snacks and drinks.
For me it was more discouraging because it felt like extra work every time I ate something. I think I would rather just pay attention to what I eat without tracking every calorie.

experience: Regularly attends concerts, markets, and local events
takeaway: Struggles to discover smaller local events because information is scattered across many social media accounts; would prefer a centralized place to find upcoming events.
quotes: Unless you follow the exact business or page hosting it, you might never see it.
There isn’t one place where I can just see everything happening that weekend.
I found out about a car show after seeing people’s pictures from it that night. That probably happens to me once or twice a month.

experience: Looks for weekend activities, concerts, and things to do with friends
takeaway: Relies heavily on word of mouth and often discovers local events too late; advance notice is an important part of their event-discovery needs.
quotes: I see stuff like that pretty often where somebody posts pictures and that’s the first time I hear about it.
It would be better if I could see upcoming events several days or even a week ahead.
Probably at least a week. That gives us enough time to see who’s going and figure out our plans.

role: UTEP student who frequently goes out with friends
experience: Regularly searches for nightlife, concerts, food, and social events
takeaway: Finds social media useful for familiar interests but wants broader event discovery and a single source that combines El Paso and Juárez events.
quotes: The problem is discovering something completely new. Social media usually keeps showing me the same type of stuff because that’s what I already interact with.
I don’t really know anywhere that combines both sides.
I missed a concert in Juárez because I saw a TikTok about it after it happened. I wasn’t following the artist.

role: College student with limited social media use

quotes: I’m sure there are more things going on, but I don’t know where they’re being advertised.

I want something that shows events by date and what’s happening this weekend.

role: College student active on social media

Instagram already puts everything in one feed for me, so it doesn’t really bother me.

experience: Event attendee

If I could sign up for a page or online service where I click on interest types, and then those would be delivered to me via email.
